title: A4 — Cost-optimized networks
bodyMarkdown:
## Cost-optimized networks

Exam task **4.4**. This lesson is the network side of cost optimization: choosing the right on-ramp to AWS, the right routing path between resources, and the right edge or throttling layer before traffic ever reaches an origin. Most network cost mistakes come from treating "it works" as good enough when a cheaper or more resilient option meets the same requirement. Each section below teaches a direct contrast so you can resolve those confusions quickly on the exam.

### K01 — AWS cost management service features (for example, cost allocation tags, multi-account billing)

Network spend is easy to lose track of unless you tag it and roll it up correctly. Cost allocation tags are the ownership control: AWS does not include your user-defined tag keys on billing reports until you activate them in Billing and Cost Management. Teams that tag NAT gateways, Transit Gateway attachments, or Direct Connect virtual interfaces still see nothing on their cost allocation report if the tag key was never activated. After you create and apply user-defined tags, it can take up to 24 hours for the tag keys to appear on your cost allocation tags page, then up to another 24 hours to activate.

For multi-account environments, consolidated billing in AWS Organizations treats the accounts in the organization as one account for the purpose of commitment discounts, so an EC2 Instance Savings Plan or Reserved Instance bought in one account can benefit matching usage in another. You can turn off Reserved Instance discount sharing on the Preferences page when chargeback policy requires strict account-level isolation. This matters for network design because centralized networking accounts (a shared Transit Gateway or Direct Connect account) often carry usage that should be billed back to the workload accounts that actually generate the traffic, and tags are how that attribution happens.

**Exam tip:** if a stem says a network resource is tagged but the tag never appears in cost reports, the missing step is activating the cost allocation tag key, not re-tagging the resource.

### K02 — AWS cost management tools with appropriate use cases (for example, AWS Cost Explorer, AWS Budgets, AWS Cost and Usage Report)

Apply the same tool-to-decision mapping here as for compute, but point it at network line items. AWS Cost Explorer lets you view data for up to the last 12 months and forecast how much you're likely to spend, which is the right tool for spotting a rising NAT gateway or data-transfer trend before it becomes a surprise. AWS Budgets lets you be alerted by email or Amazon SNS notification when actual or forecasted cost and usage exceed your budget threshold, which is the right tool for a hard ceiling on a specific network resource or account. The Cost and Usage Report contains a comprehensive set of AWS cost and usage data, including the granular usage types (per-GB NAT processing, per-GB inter-Region transfer, per-attachment-hour Transit Gateway charges) that Cost Explorer's dashboards summarize away.

The confusion to avoid is using Cost Explorer as an alerting tool or CUR as a dashboard. Cost Explorer explains a trend after the fact and forecasts forward; it does not page anyone. Budgets is the only one of the three built to notify or act automatically. CUR is the raw dataset for a custom query when you need to isolate exactly which subnet, resource, or usage type is driving a NAT or data-transfer bill.

**Exam tip:** "forecast the trend" points to Cost Explorer, "notify before a threshold is crossed" points to Budgets, and "line-item detail by usage type" points to CUR.

### K03 — Load balancing concepts (for example, Application Load Balancer [ALB])

A load balancer is also a network cost decision, not just an availability one. Application Load Balancer operates at the application layer (layer 7) and is the right fit when you need host-based or path-based routing across HTTP or HTTPS microservices, because it lets you run one load balancer in front of many backend services instead of one per service. Network Load Balancer (NLB) operates at the transport layer (layer 4) and is built for raw TCP or UDP throughput and static IP addresses; Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB) operates at the network layer (layer 3) and is built for inserting a fleet of virtual security appliances transparently into a traffic path.

The cost-optimization angle is picking the cheapest layer that satisfies the requirement instead of defaulting to ALB everywhere. If the requirement is only "distribute TCP connections to a fixed set of backend instances with a stable IP that a partner has allowlisted," an NLB avoids the extra application-layer processing and rule evaluation that ALB is priced and built for. If the requirement is "route /api and /images to different target groups on the same domain," only ALB's Layer 7 routing does that without a second load balancer.

**Exam tip:** match the layer named in the requirement (HTTP routing rules, raw TCP throughput, or appliance insertion) to ALB, NLB, or GWLB before considering price; the wrong layer cannot be made cheaper by resizing it.

### K04 — NAT gateways (for example, NAT instance costs compared with NAT gateway costs)

NAT gateway and NAT instance solve the same problem, outbound internet access for private subnets, with very different cost and operational models. A NAT gateway is charged for each hour that it is available and each gigabyte of data that it processes; AWS documentation states plainly that they provide better availability and bandwidth and require less effort on your part to administer. A NAT instance instead is charged depending on the number of NAT instances that you use, duration of usage, and instance type and size, which means its cost is really EC2 pricing, so it can be cheaper for a small, predictable, low-throughput workload but only if you accept that you manage its patching, sizing, and failover yourself.

The scale point matters: a NAT gateway can scale up to 100 Gbps automatically, while a NAT instance's bandwidth is capped by whatever instance type you chose, and scaling it means resizing or replacing the instance. For most production workloads on the exam, NAT gateway is the default correct answer specifically because it removes an operational burden that has a real cost even when the EC2 bill looks smaller.

**Exam tip:** "least operational overhead" plus "NAT" almost always means NAT gateway; only pick a NAT instance when the stem explicitly calls for a bastion host, port forwarding, or a security-group-level control that a NAT gateway does not support.

### K05 — Network connectivity (for example, private lines, dedicated lines, VPNs)

Three connectivity classes cover most hybrid scenarios: the public internet, a Site-to-Site VPN over the internet, and AWS Direct Connect as a private, dedicated line. Direct Connect bypasses the public internet and establishes a direct, private connection between your on-premises network and AWS, which gives consistent latency and throughput that ordinary internet paths cannot guarantee. A dedicated Direct Connect connection comes with bandwidths of 1 Gbps, 10 Gbps, 100 Gbps, or 400 Gbps, while a hosted connection through an AWS Direct Connect Partner offers available bandwidths from 50 Mbps up to 25 Gbps for customers who do not need a full dedicated port.

Site-to-Site VPN is faster to provision and cheaper to start, but it rides over the internet, so its latency and jitter are not guaranteed the way Direct Connect's are. Each Site-to-Site VPN connection has two tunnels, with each tunnel using a unique public IP address, which gives you redundancy but not a dedicated physical path. The plain public internet is the default for anything that does not need a private network relationship with AWS at all.

**Exam tip:** "consistent, predictable, dedicated bandwidth to AWS" points to Direct Connect; "quick to set up, no physical cross-connect, still needs encryption over the internet" points to Site-to-Site VPN.

### K06 — Network routing, topology, and peering (for example, AWS Transit Gateway, VPC peering)

VPC peering and Transit Gateway both connect VPCs, but they scale differently and price differently. There is no charge to create a VPC peering connection, and all data transfer over a VPC peering connection that stays within an Availability Zone is free; charges apply for data transfer over VPC peering connections that cross Availability Zones and Regions. Peering is a direct, one-to-one connection with no single point of failure or bandwidth bottleneck, but it does not transit, meaning VPC A peered with VPC B and VPC B peered with VPC C does not let A reach C.

Transit Gateway is a network transit hub used to interconnect VPCs and on-premises networks, and it is billed separately for each VPC attachment-hour and for the data it processes, similar to the "AWS Transit Gateway (VPC attachment)" and "AWS Transit Gateway (data processed)" line items that appear on an AWS cost breakdown. Choose peering for a small, static number of VPCs that need direct low-cost connectivity. Choose Transit Gateway once you have enough VPCs, VPNs, or Direct Connect gateways that a full mesh of peering connections would become unmanageable, even though Transit Gateway adds its own per-attachment and per-GB charges that a two-VPC peering connection would not have.

**Exam tip:** a handful of VPCs that need direct connectivity favors peering's lower cost; a growing hub-and-spoke topology favors Transit Gateway's manageability even at a higher per-GB price.

### K07 — Network services with appropriate use cases (for example, DNS)

DNS is the network service most exam scenarios take for granted until a question hinges on it. A DNS service such as Amazon Route 53 makes the connection between domain names and IP addresses, which is what lets a user type a domain name instead of an IP address and reach the correct resource, potentially across multiple Regions or providers behind health checks and routing policies.

Cost-optimized network service selection also depends on distinguishing DNS from performance and delivery services that solve adjacent problems. DNS resolves a name to an endpoint; it does not cache content, encrypt traffic, or reduce data transfer volume by itself. Routing policies such as latency-based or geolocation routing can direct users to the nearest or cheapest Regional endpoint, which indirectly reduces cross-Region data transfer, but the DNS lookup itself is not what moves the bytes.

**Exam tip:** if the requirement is "resolve a name to the nearest healthy endpoint," that is a Route 53 routing-policy question, not a load-balancer or CDN question.

### S01 — Configuring appropriate NAT gateway types for a network (for example, a single shared NAT gateway compared with NAT gateways for each Availability Zone)

A NAT gateway operates within a designated Availability Zone and is built with redundancy in that AZ only, so a single shared NAT gateway is a resilience and, indirectly, a cost trade-off: if that AZ has an outage, private-subnet resources in every other AZ that route through it also lose internet access, and any cross-AZ traffic to reach it is billed as inter-AZ data transfer. Placing a NAT gateway in each Availability Zone with resources removes both problems: it keeps traffic in-AZ and keeps one AZ's failure from taking down egress (outbound internet traffic) for the whole VPC.

The trade-off is that a NAT gateway is charged for each hour it is available, so per-AZ NAT gateways multiply that hourly charge by however many AZs you cover. A cost-optimized design still defaults to one NAT gateway per AZ for production because the hourly charge is small compared with the cross-AZ data-processing charges and the availability risk of a single shared gateway; a single shared NAT gateway is only appropriate for a non-production or low-traffic VPC where that trade-off is acceptable.

**Exam tip:** "resources in one Availability Zone must not lose internet access if another Availability Zone fails" is the signal for one NAT gateway per AZ, not a single shared NAT gateway.

### S02 — Configuring appropriate network connections (for example, AWS Direct Connect compared with VPN compared with internet)

Configuring the connection means matching the requirement's latency, bandwidth, and security language to one of the three options from K05. If the requirement calls out a need for a dedicated line, consistent latency, or a guaranteed bandwidth of 1 Gbps or higher for sustained hybrid traffic, Direct Connect bypasses the public internet and establishes a direct, private connection between your on-premises network and AWS, which is the only option built for that guarantee.

If the requirement instead calls for encrypted connectivity that can be stood up in hours rather than weeks (a Direct Connect cross-connect takes provisioning time with a partner or AWS), a Site-to-Site VPN over the internet is the fit, and you can also run a VPN as a backup path over an existing Direct Connect connection for resilience. If there is no stated requirement for a private network relationship with AWS at all, for example a public API endpoint reachable from anywhere, the public internet with TLS is the correct, and cheapest, connection.

**Exam tip:** "needs guaranteed bandwidth or consistent latency" means Direct Connect; "needs encrypted connectivity fast, with no physical circuit" means VPN; "no hybrid requirement stated" means plain internet.

### S03 — Configuring appropriate network routes to minimize network transfer costs (for example, Region to Region, Availability Zone to Availability Zone, private to public, AWS Global Accelerator, VPC endpoints)

This skill is about removing unnecessary hops and unnecessary public-internet or cross-boundary transfer. Data transfers between AWS Regions typically incur charges, so a cost-optimized design avoids a multi-Region path unless the workload specifically requires it. Inside a Region, keeping AZ-to-AZ traffic to a minimum (for example, placing a NAT gateway in the same AZ as the resources that use it, as covered in S01) avoids the same class of charge at a smaller scale.

VPC endpoints remove the need to route to AWS services over the internet or through a NAT gateway at all. The selection rule is direct: use a gateway endpoint when the target is Amazon S3 or DynamoDB, because there is no additional charge for using gateway endpoints; use an interface endpoint, which relies on AWS PrivateLink and is billed at standard PrivateLink rates, for any other AWS service that supports it. Consider creating an interface endpoint or gateway endpoint for services that receive most of your NAT gateway's traffic, which removes that traffic from the NAT gateway's per-GB processing charge entirely. AWS Global Accelerator is a different tool for a different job: its static IP addresses accept incoming traffic onto the AWS global network from the edge location closest to your users, which improves performance and availability for TCP and UDP traffic, but it is not primarily a cost-reduction tool the way a gateway endpoint or CloudFront is.

**Exam tip:** "eliminate NAT or internet gateway data-processing charges for S3 or DynamoDB traffic" is a gateway endpoint question; "improve global TCP/UDP performance with static entry-point IPs" is a Global Accelerator question, not a cost-minimization one.

### S04 — Determining strategic needs for content delivery networks (CDNs) and edge caching

A CDN is the highest-leverage network cost tool for content that many users request repeatedly. Amazon CloudFront speeds up content delivery by leveraging its global network of data centers, known as edge locations, and it costs less to deliver your content from CloudFront points-of-presence than directly from Regions. CloudFront also does not charge origin retrieval fees for AWS-based origins such as Amazon EC2 and Amazon S3, so once an object is cached at the edge, repeated requests stop generating origin data-transfer charges at all.

The strategic decision is recognizing which workloads benefit: static or infrequently changing assets (images, video segments, software downloads, static site content) cache well and see the largest savings. Highly dynamic, per-user, uncacheable API responses benefit less from caching but can still benefit from CloudFront's reduced-cost path to the AWS network for the connection itself. When multiple CDNs sit in front of the same origin, CloudFront Origin Shield adds an additional caching layer in front of the origin to consolidate requests from the different providers and further reduce origin load.

CloudFront caches and accelerates HTTP and HTTPS content only. A non-HTTP application, such as a custom TCP/UDP protocol, a multiplayer game backend, or VoIP traffic, that still needs a fixed entry-point IP address is a Global Accelerator scenario, not a CloudFront one, because Global Accelerator operates on TCP and UDP traffic generally rather than caching HTTP objects.

**Exam tip:** "reduce repeated download cost for the same static content across a global audience" is a CDN and edge-caching question answered by putting CloudFront in front of the origin; "fixed entry-point IP for a non-HTTP protocol" is a Global Accelerator question instead.

### S05 — Reviewing existing workloads for network optimizations

Reviewing a live workload for network cost issues starts with visibility, not guessing. Use Amazon CloudWatch and VPC flow logs to capture details about your data transfer and network usage, and use metering and reporting tools such as AWS Cost Explorer, CUDOS Dashboards, or CloudWatch to understand the data transfer cost of your workload. That visibility is what tells you whether the biggest line item is cross-Region transfer, NAT gateway processing, or a chatty AZ-to-AZ pattern, because the fix is different for each one.

Once you know where the transfer is going, the review checklist mirrors S01 through S04: confirm NAT gateways sit in the same AZ as the resources that use them, confirm VPC endpoints exist for the AWS services that generate the most NAT traffic, confirm cross-Region calls are actually required, and confirm cacheable content is in front of a CDN. Avoid transferring data across Regional boundaries unless it is a very thoughtful decision, since AWS treats a multi-Region path as something to justify, not a default.

**Exam tip:** a "review an existing architecture for network savings" scenario is answered by naming the specific monitoring tool that reveals the cost driver, then the specific S01–S04 fix for that driver, not by a vague "optimize the network" answer.

### S06 — Selecting an appropriate throttling strategy

Throttling protects both availability and cost by rejecting excess requests before they consume downstream compute or generate downstream charges. Amazon API Gateway throttles requests to your API using the token bucket algorithm, where a token counts for a request, and when request submissions exceed the steady-state rate and burst limits, clients may receive `429 Too Many Requests` error responses. Account-level and stage-level throttling protect the whole account or API by default; on top of that, you can enable usage plans to set throttles on client request submissions based on specified request rates and quotas, which lets you give different API keys or customer tiers different limits.

The strategy choice depends on who you are protecting from what. A stage-level or method-level throttle protects your backend and its cost from any client, including your own traffic spikes. A usage plan protects you from a specific external client or tier exceeding its contracted rate, and it is the mechanism for turning "customers on the free tier get 10 requests per second" into an enforced limit rather than a support conversation.

**Exam tip:** "limit every caller uniformly to protect the backend" is a stage or account-level throttle; "give different customers or API keys different limits" is a usage plan.

### S07 — Selecting the appropriate bandwidth allocation for a network device (for example, a single VPN compared with multiple VPNs, Direct Connect speed)

Bandwidth allocation means picking a number, not just a service. For Site-to-Site VPN, standard bandwidth is up to 1.25 Gbps per tunnel by default, and a Large Bandwidth Tunnel raises that to up to 5 Gbps per tunnel, though Large Bandwidth Tunnels are available only for VPN connections attached to Transit Gateway or Cloud WAN. A single standard VPN connection tops out well below most sustained hybrid workloads, which is why a workload that needs more throughput than one tunnel provides is scaled with multiple VPN connections in parallel (using equal-cost multi-path routing through Transit Gateway) rather than by assuming one tunnel will stretch further than its ceiling.

For Direct Connect, a dedicated connection comes in 1 Gbps, 10 Gbps, 100 Gbps, or 400 Gbps increments, while a hosted connection through a Direct Connect Partner is available from 50 Mbps up to 25 Gbps, which fits customers who need more than a VPN's ceiling but less than a full dedicated port. Right-sizing this allocation matters for cost because a 10 Gbps dedicated port billed by the hour costs the same whether it carries 100 Mbps or 9 Gbps of real traffic, so the size should match measured or projected peak demand, not a guess.

**Exam tip:** when a stem gives you a required throughput number, match it to the smallest VPN tunnel count or Direct Connect port size that clears that number, not the largest option available.

### Warnings

- Do not use the AWS root user for routine lab work.
- Stopping an instance is not teardown.
- $10 budget alerts warn; they do not stop spend.
